1 · Read the explanation.
One property, three consequences

Whether a noun is countable in English is not a fact about the world; it is a fact about the word. Once you know it, three things follow automatically.

The plural. Countable nouns have one; uncountable nouns do not. Two communities, but never two researches. The article. A singular countable noun must have one: a community, the community. An uncountable noun takes none when it is general, and the when it is specific: support is free, but the support she got was excellent. The quantifier. Many, a few and several go with countable nouns; much, a little and a great deal of go with uncountable ones.

The words that catch learners out
  • Uncountable in English, countable in many other languages: research, advice, information, equipment, furniture, permission, support, homework, news, progress.
  • To count them, use a unit word: a piece of research, a word of advice, an item of equipment.
  • The verb is singular: research suggests, the news is, this information is.
  • Some nouns are both, with different meanings: a paper (an article) and paper (the material); a coffee (a cup) and coffee (the drink); an experience (an event) and experience (what you have learned).

Two things to watch

1 — A singular countable noun is never bare. She joined community is not possible. It needs a, the, this, her or another determiner. Uncountable nouns can stand alone, and that is the difference learners most often miss.

2 — The adverb goes with the verb, not the noun. Numbers rose dramatically, not numbers rose dramatic. Before an adjective, the adverb comes first: significantly higher, noticeably quieter.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Countability is a grammatical decision, not a fact about the world

Whether a noun can be counted decides four things at once: whether it has a plural, which article it takes, which quantifier goes in front of it and whether the verb is singular or plural. Research suggests that numbers are rising — singular verb, no article, no plural. researches, a research and many research are all the same error seen from different sides.

The trap is that English does not always agree with other languages about which nouns are countable. Advice, information, research, support, permission, equipment, furniture, luggage, news, progress, accommodation, work are uncountable in English whatever they are in Russian or Kazakh. To count them you need a unit: a piece of research, a word of advice, two items of equipment.

The same word, both ways

Many nouns are countable in one meaning and uncountable in another, and the article tells the reader which you mean. She has plenty of experience (knowledge built up) against It was an experience I will not repeat (one event). There is no room left (space) against a room with two windows. Also: time / a time, paper / a paper, business / a business, coffee / a coffee.

Uncountable nouns still take the when you narrow them: Research suggests… in general, but The research she published was clear. That is the same general-against-particular test as the article lesson.

Errors to watch: informations, advices, equipments → no plural · a good news → good news or a piece of good news · The news are bad → The news is bad · many research → a great deal of research · She gave me an advice → a piece of advice.

It must do something the town cannot already do, it must be useful to people who are isolated socially or cannot travel, and somebody has to keep it running. 1 · Read the model.
Model · a proposal to the library

We propose an online community for carers — the people who look after a parent or a husband or wife at home, full time and mostly alone. There are, according to recent research, about four hundred of them in this town, and hardly any support available to them locally.

The group would do three things. It would let members ask practical questions at two in the morning, which is when most of them are awake. It would carry a list of what is available in the district, since a great deal of that information exists and almost none of it is in one place. And it would organise one meeting a month in the library itself, for anybody who can get out of the house.

It needs very little equipment and no permission from anybody. It needs one moderator, paid for four hours a week, and somebody who will not lose interest in the second year. That, rather than the technology, is what such groups usually fail on. Membership elsewhere has grown noticeably wherever a paid moderator was kept.
